## Introduction

Education is strongly associated with labor market outcomes, but the size of that relationship depends on what we measure. Are education gaps mainly about **unemployment among people who are already in the labor force**, or are they larger when we look at **whether people participate in the labor market at all**?

This post uses IPUMS CPS Basic Monthly Survey microdata to compare adults ages 25–64 across four education groups. I use July samples from 2015 through 2026 and calculate population statistics using the CPS final person weight, `WTFINL`.

I restrict the sample to ages 25–64 to focus on working-age adults who have largely completed their education. Educational attainment is grouped into four categories: high school or less, some college or an associate degree, a bachelor’s degree, and a graduate degree. The unemployment rate is calculated only among people in the labor force, while the labor force participation rate measures the share of the working-age population that is either employed or actively looking for work.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ipumsr)
library(scales)

ddi <- read_ipums_ddi("data/raw/cps_00001.xml")

cps <- read_ipums_micro(
  ddi,
  data_file = "data/raw/cps_00001.dat.gz"
)

cps_clean <- cps |>
  filter(AGE >= 25, AGE <= 64) |>
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      EDUC <= 73 ~ "High school or less",
      EDUC > 73 & EDUC < 111 ~ "Some college / Associate",
      EDUC == 111 ~ "Bachelor's degree",
      EDUC > 111 & EDUC < 999 ~ "Graduate degree",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(education))
```

```{r}
unemp_trend <- cps_clean |>
  filter(LABFORCE == 2) |>
  mutate(
    unemployed = EMPSTAT >= 20 & EMPSTAT < 30
  ) |>
  group_by(YEAR, education) |>
  summarise(
    unemployment_rate = weighted.mean(
      unemployed,
      w = WTFINL,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

lfp_trend <- cps_clean |>
  mutate(
    in_labor_force = LABFORCE == 2
  ) |>
  group_by(YEAR, education) |>
  summarise(
    labor_force_participation = weighted.mean(
      in_labor_force,
      w = WTFINL,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## Unemployment Gaps Are Persistent but Relatively Modest

The unemployment rate is consistently higher for adults with less education, but the size of the gap is usually fairly small.

```{r}
unemp_trend |>
  mutate(
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(
        "High school or less",
        "Some college / Associate",
        "Bachelor's degree",
        "Graduate degree"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = YEAR,
      y = unemployment_rate,
      color = education
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2015:2026
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Unemployment Rate by Education, July 2015–2026",
    subtitle = "Adults ages 25–64",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Unemployment rate",
    color = "Education",
    caption = "Source: IPUMS CPS"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

The ordering is clear across most years: adults with less education tend to have higher unemployment. The gap widened sharply during the COVID-19 labor market disruption in July 2020, when less-educated workers experienced a much larger increase in unemployment. By July 2026, however, unemployment ranged from about **4.4% for adults with a high school education or less to 2.6% for adults with graduate degrees**, a difference of only about **1.7 percentage points**.

## Participation Gaps Are Much Larger

The education differences become much larger when the outcome is labor force participation rather than unemployment.

```{r}
lfp_trend |>
  mutate(
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(
        "High school or less",
        "Some college / Associate",
        "Bachelor's degree",
        "Graduate degree"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = YEAR,
      y = labor_force_participation,
      color = education
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2015:2026
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Labor Force Participation by Education, July 2015–2026",
    subtitle = "Adults ages 25–64",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Labor force participation rate",
    color = "Education",
    caption = "Source: IPUMS CPS"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

Unlike the unemployment gap, the participation gap is large and persistent. In July 2026, about **71.1%** of adults with a high school education or less were in the labor force, compared with **87.7%** of adults with graduate degrees. That is a gap of about **16.6 percentage points**.

This difference is important because the unemployment rate only describes people who are already participating in the labor market. Someone who is not working and not actively looking for work is not counted as unemployed.

## The Main Education Gap Is in Participation

To compare the two outcomes directly, I calculate the gap between adults with a high school education or less and adults with graduate degrees. For unemployment, the gap is the lower-education group’s unemployment rate minus the graduate-degree group’s rate. For participation, the gap is the graduate-degree group’s participation rate minus the lower-education group’s rate.

```{r}
gap_trend <- unemp_trend |>
  select(YEAR, education, unemployment_rate) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = education,
    values_from = unemployment_rate
  ) |>
  transmute(
    YEAR,
    unemployment_gap =
      (`High school or less` - `Graduate degree`) * 100
  ) |>
  left_join(
    lfp_trend |>
      select(YEAR, education, labor_force_participation) |>
      pivot_wider(
        names_from = education,
        values_from = labor_force_participation
      ) |>
      transmute(
        YEAR,
        participation_gap =
          (`Graduate degree` - `High school or less`) * 100
      ),
    by = "YEAR"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(unemployment_gap, participation_gap),
    names_to = "outcome",
    values_to = "gap_pp"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    outcome = recode(
      outcome,
      unemployment_gap = "Unemployment gap",
      participation_gap = "Participation gap"
    )
  )

gap_trend |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = YEAR,
      y = gap_pp,
      color = outcome
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2015:2026
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Education Gaps Are Much Larger for Labor Force Participation",
    subtitle = "Gap between high school or less and graduate degree, in percentage points",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Percentage-point gap",
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Source: IPUMS CPS"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

This comparison ties the two outcomes together. From 2015 through 2026, the participation gap stayed around **16–19 percentage points**, while the unemployment gap was usually only about **1–4 percentage points**, except for a larger spike during 2020.

The implication is that the largest education difference in these data is not simply who finds a job among people already in the labor force. It is **who participates in the labor market in the first place**.

## Conclusion

Education is associated with both unemployment and labor force participation, but the two relationships are very different in size. Adults with less education generally have higher unemployment, especially during labor market disruptions such as 2020. However, the much larger and more persistent gap is in labor force participation.

For July 2026, the unemployment gap between adults with a high school education or less and those with graduate degrees was about **1.7 percentage points**, compared with a **16.6 percentage-point participation gap**. This suggests that the main labor market difference across these education groups is participation rather than unemployment conditional on being in the labor force.

These patterns are descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal effects of education.

## Data Source

Data are from IPUMS CPS Basic Monthly samples. The extract contains July observations from 2015 through 2026.
